g.title: have: lexical and grammatical uses
g.rule:
Have works as a main verb, an auxiliary and part of several structures.

main verb: possession (no continuous) · action (continuous possible)I have two sisters. · We're having a family dinner.
have got: informal, present onlyShe's got her father's eyes.
have to / have got toI've got to call my mother.
have something doneWe had the family photos framed.

ex.q: We ___ a huge row last night.
I'm going to ___.
o: have cut my hair by someone

ex.q: Do we ___ to invite all the relatives?

talk: Which of your relatives are you most alike, in looks and in character?
How has the role of the family changed in your country?

r.text:
I have two sisters, and I have had forty years to think about what that means. I am the middle one, which, according to popular psychology, should have made me a diplomat.

It hasn't. What I have got instead is an unusually accurate memory for injustice. My elder sister had her own room; I had to share. My younger sister had her homework checked; I had mine ignored. We have had this argument at every family gathering since 1998, and nobody has ever won it.

And yet, when our father fell ill last year, something shifted. We had the house to clear and decisions to make. The bossy one turned out to be resourceful. The moody one was the most reliable. I, the supposedly open-minded one, was stubborn about every teaspoon.

We had the furniture valued and found that none of it was worth anything. What we had, it turned out, was each other, and a shared language of thirty-year-old grievances that nobody else on earth can speak.

ex.q: What position does the writer hold in the family?
What does she say she has instead of diplomacy?
The sisters stopped arguing in 1998.
What did they discover when their father fell ill?

l.intro: Two cousins talk at a family gathering.

script.t: Ruslan, have you got a minute? I've been having a strange conversation with Aunt Roza.
Let me guess. She's had another idea about the family business.
She has. She wants us to have the old shop redecorated before spring.
She's always been assertive. Bossy, some would say.
We have to admit she's reliable, though. She's had that shop running for thirty years.
True. And you've got her stubborn streak, if you don't mind my saying so.
I'd rather call it being conscientious. Have you got any better ideas?
We could have a designer look at it. I haven't got the patience myself.
You've never had any. That's the one trait we don't share.
Fair enough. Shall we have a word with her together?

ex.q: What does Aunt Roza want?
How does Ruslan describe his aunt?
Dana accepts that she is stubborn.
What do they decide to do?

g.title: Discourse markers (1): linkers
g.rule:
Linkers signal how two ideas are related; formal writing uses different ones from speech.

resultso · as a result · consequently · therefore
reasonbecause · as / since · due to / owing to + noun
purposeto · in order to · so as not to · so that
contrastbut · yet · however · nevertheless · whereas · despite

ex.q: The firm lost its biggest client. ___, forty staff were made redundant.
The flight was cancelled ___ fog.
I left early so ___ not to miss the train.

talk: What makes a job satisfying? Rank salary, colleagues, security and freedom, and justify your order.
Would you rather work for yourself or for a company? Why?

r.text:
Every profession has an image problem, but few have one as severe as lighthouse keeping. The work is solitary, repetitive and, on most coasts, obsolete, since the lamps are now automatic. Nevertheless, when a remote island advertised for a keeper last year, more than two thousand people applied.

The salary was modest, and the post offered no career ladder whatsoever. Consequently, the trust that runs the island expected a handful of eccentrics. Instead it received applications from lawyers, surgeons and a head teacher.

Why? Several candidates said that their high-powered jobs had become tedious in spite of the status. Others wanted demanding physical work, whereas their current roles kept them at a screen. Almost all mentioned silence.

The successful applicant, a former accountant, has now completed her first winter. She describes the work as rewarding, yet she is realistic. "It is not an escape. The roof still leaks, the paperwork still exists, and owing to the weather I have not seen another person since February. However, I have stopped checking my phone. There is nothing on it."

ex.q: Why is lighthouse keeping mostly obsolete?
How many people applied?
Most applicants were unemployed eccentrics.
What does the new keeper say about the job?

l.intro: A careers adviser talks to a graduate.

script.t: So you've been job hunting for six months. How is it going?
Slowly. I've had interviews; however, nothing has come of them so far.
Why do you think that is?
Partly owing to my lack of experience. Besides, I've only applied for high-powered positions.
That may be the problem. A less demanding role would let you learn, whereas a senior one expects results immediately.
I don't want a dead-end job, though.
Nor should you. Nevertheless, a repetitive first year is often rewarding later.
So as not to waste time, should I retrain?
Not yet. Since your degree is strong, I'd widen the search instead.
All right. Consequently, I'll be applying for things I used to ignore.

ex.q: How long has she been job hunting?
What does the adviser see as the problem?
o: She only applies for senior roles

ex.q: The adviser tells her to retrain immediately.
What will she do now?

lessons.title: Reading: The job nobody applies for

g.title: The past: habitual events and specific incidents
g.rule:
Separate what regularly happened from what happened once.

repeated actionsWe would spend every summer at my gran's. · I used to climb that tree.
past states: used to, not wouldI used to be terrified of the dark.
one incident: narrative tensesOne day I fell while I was climbing; I had been told not to.

ex.q: As a child I ___ very shy.
Every Sunday my grandfather ___ us stories.
One morning I ___ (wake) up and the house was empty.

talk: Describe your earliest memory in as much detail as you can.
What did you regularly do as a child that children today rarely do?

r.text:
My primary school had four classrooms and a stove, and for six years I would walk there every morning along a road that no longer exists.

Our teacher was a tall woman who used to keep a ruler in her sleeve. She never hit anybody with it. She would simply let it slide into her hand when the noise grew, and thirty children would fall silent. We used to believe she could hear thoughts.

We would recite poems on Mondays and wash the floor on Fridays. In winter the ink would freeze, and we were allowed to keep our coats on.

One morning in my last year she did not come. A stranger arrived instead and told us that she had been taken to hospital during the night. We had prepared a poem for her; we recited it to the empty chair.

She returned in spring, thinner, and I was reading by the window when she came in. She looked at the class, let the ruler slide into her hand out of habit, and then, for the first time, laughed.

ex.q: What did the teacher keep in her sleeve?
What happened in winter?
The teacher often hit the children.
What did the children do when she was in hospital?
o: Recited the poem to the empty chair

l.intro: A writer remembers her childhood for a radio programme.

script.t: You write a great deal about your childhood. What do you remember most clearly?
The summers. We would spend every August at my grandfather's house in the mountains.
What did you use to do there?
He would wake us at five and we'd walk to the river. I used to hate it at the time.
Was there ever a moment of real freedom?
One morning I slipped out alone. I had been told never to cross the bridge, and of course I crossed it.
What happened?
I was standing in the middle when a storm broke. I had never felt such fear, or such curiosity.
Did your grandfather find out?
He was waiting on the other side. He didn't say a word, which was worse than any punishment.

ex.q: Where did the writer spend every August?
As a child she enjoyed getting up at five.
What had she been told not to do?
How did her grandfather react?

lessons.title: The past: habitual events and specific incidents

g.title: Pronouns
g.rule:
Small words that are easy to get wrong at an advanced level.

generic: you, one, theyYou never know. · One should be careful. · They say it's hard.
reflexive and emphaticI taught myself. · The director herself replied.
each other / one anotherThey don't speak to each other.
it and there as empty subjectsIt's hard to say. · There seems to be a problem.

ex.q: If someone calls, tell ___ I'm out.
My parents taught ___ English from films.
___ is no point in arguing.

talk: Which language would you most like to learn, and how would you teach yourself?
Do the languages people speak change how they think? Discuss.

r.text:
Every language has gaps. English has no single word for the day after tomorrow, and it has had to borrow from other languages to describe the pleasure one takes in somebody else's misfortune.

Translators live in these gaps. One of them told me that she had spent a week on a single Kazakh term of respect, which one uses for an older relative and which carries warmth that "aunt" or "uncle" simply lacks. In the end she left it as it was and trusted readers to work it out for themselves.

One might assume that a missing word means a missing idea. It doesn't. They say that speakers of every language can describe anything; it merely takes some of them longer. What differs is what a language makes you notice. If yours forces you to mark whether you saw something yourself or only heard about it, you become rather careful about gossip.

The translator put it better. "Nobody thinks in a dictionary. We think, and then each of us reaches for whatever our own language happens to have left lying around."

ex.q: What does English lack a single word for?
What did the translator do with the Kazakh term?
A missing word means the idea cannot be expressed.
What does a language influence, according to the text?

l.intro: Two colleagues discuss learning a language as an adult.

script.t: Peter, they say you never lose an accent after childhood. Is it true?
It depends who you ask. One can improve it, but it rarely disappears.
I taught myself Italian last year. It was harder than I'd expected.
Did you find yourself translating everything?
Constantly. There's no synonym for half the words I need.
It's the irregular verbs that defeat me. My siblings and I used to test each other.
Did you really? My husband and I correct one another all the time.
You can't expect to sound like a native. Nobody does.
I'd settle for being understood. They say that's what matters.
It is. And there's nothing wrong with a little accent of your own.

ex.q: What does Peter say about accents?
o: They can improve but rarely disappear

ex.q: How did Aigerim learn Italian?
Peter finds irregular verbs easy.
What would Aigerim settle for?

lessons.title: Reading: A word that isn't there
Speaking: On the tip of my tongue

words: Develop a close connection with someone
Deliberately trying to make people react strongly
Saying the opposite of what you mean, to mock
Have a good relationship with someone
Find out what someone is really like
get the wrong end of the stick
Make other people do what you want
Do something wrong without being caught
Throw away or remove something you don’t want
get on like a house on fire
Become friends very quickly and easily

g.title: get
g.rule:
Get has many meanings; the structure tells you which.

becomeIt's getting late. · They got engaged.
passive (informal)He got fired.
get someone to do = persuadeI got him to apologise.
get something done = arrangeI must get my phone fixed.

ex.q: I finally ___ her to tell me the truth.
We need to ___ before winter.
They ___ (get) married last spring.

talk: What qualities make a relationship last? Give examples from people you know.
Describe a historical period or event you love or hate reading about.

r.text:
History is full of friendships that began badly. Most of us can name two neighbours or colleagues who loathed each other for years before they finally got round to having a proper conversation.

Why do some enmities turn? A psychologist who studies conflict suggests that strong dislike requires attention, and that attention is, awkwardly, the raw material of intimacy. You cannot get to know somebody without thinking about them, and nobody thinks about us more than our rivals.

She describes two colleagues who could not get through a meeting without a sarcastic exchange. Then one of them got ill. The other got the job of covering her work, got hold of her files, and got a shock: they were brilliant. By the time she got back, he had got over his aversion entirely.

It doesn't always work. Some people simply get on each other's nerves for life. But it is worth remembering, the next time somebody gets the wrong end of the stick about you, that indifference would be far more final.

ex.q: What does strong dislike require, according to the psychologist?
What changed the colleague's mind?
All enmities eventually turn into friendship.
What would be 'far more final' than dislike?

l.intro: Two friends talk about a difficult flatmate.

script.t: How are you getting on with your new flatmate?
Badly. I think she got the wrong end of the stick on day one.
What happened?
I asked her to turn the music down and she got really upset.
Have you tried to get to know her?
I've tried. I can't get her to talk about anything but work.
It gets easier. My brother and I used to loathe each other.
I'm getting tired of her sarcastic comments, though.
Get her to cook with you. Food is the quickest way to bond.
I'll try. If it gets any worse, I'm getting the lock changed.

ex.q: How is Sofia getting on with her flatmate?
What upset the flatmate?
o: Being asked to turn the music down

ex.q: Jamie has always got on well with his brother.
What does Jamie suggest?

g.title: Discourse markers (2): adverbs and adverbial expressions
g.rule:
These expressions show your attitude or organise what you say.

being honest or giving an opinionto be honest · frankly · as far as I'm concerned
adding or changing directionbesides · anyway · by the way · as for the acting
correcting or clarifyingin fact · actually · I mean · in other words
generalising and concludingon the whole · basically · all in all

ex.q: ___, did you ever finish that novel?
The plot was thin. ___, the acting was superb.
As far as I'm ___, the book was better.

talk: Review a film or series based on real events. Was it accurate, and does that matter?
Should film-makers be free to change history?

r.text:
Historical drama has never been more popular, and historians have never been more irritated. Basically, the complaint is always the same: the costumes are perfect and the facts are not.

To be fair, screenwriters have a real problem. In reality, a siege lasts months and consists largely of waiting. On screen, obviously, something has to happen before the adverts. As a result, treaties are signed in an afternoon and generals who never met exchange memorable insults.

Does it matter? As far as entertainment is concerned, probably not. On the other hand, surveys suggest that most people's knowledge of the past now comes from television. In other words, the invented scene becomes the remembered one.

Some directors, incidentally, have found a compromise: they film the legend and then, at the end, state plainly what is known. Admittedly, few viewers read it.

All in all, the historians might consider a different approach. After all, a drama that sends one viewer in a hundred to the library has, arguably, done more for history than a footnote ever did.

ex.q: What is the historians' usual complaint?
Why do screenwriters change events?
o: Real events are slow and something must happen

ex.q: Most people now learn about the past from books.
What compromise have some directors found?
o: Stating what is known at the end

l.intro: Two students review a historical drama for their podcast.

script.t: So, the new series about the siege. Was it any good?
To be honest, I had mixed feelings. Visually, it was stunning.
As far as accuracy is concerned, though?
Basically, they invented half the characters. In fact, the treaty scene never happened.
Does that matter? After all, it's drama, not a lecture.
Up to a point. On the other hand, viewers will believe the civilians were never warned.
As for the acting, I thought the general was superb.
Admittedly, he was. Anyway, would you recommend it?
On the whole, yes. Incidentally, there's a documentary on the same events.
All in all, watch both and decide for yourselves.

ex.q: What did Luke think of the series visually?
What is his main criticism?
Zarina thought the actor playing the general was poor.
What is their final advice?
o: Watch both the series and the documentary

lessons.title: Discourse markers (2): adverbs and adverbial expressions

g.title: Adding emphasis (1): inversion
g.rule:
After a negative or limiting expression at the start, invert subject and auxiliary. This is formal.

Never / Rarely / SeldomNever have I read such a moving book.
Not only … but alsoNot only did she write it, she also illustrated it.
Hardly / No soonerNo sooner had I started than the phone rang.
Only then / Not untilNot until the last page did I understand.

ex.q: Rarely ___ such a gripping opening chapter.
No sooner had we sat down ___ the lights went out.
Not only ___ he write the book, he also published it himself.

talk: Recommend a book and say why. Try to use one or two emphatic sentences.
Do you prefer paper books, e-books or audiobooks? Why?

r.text:
Never have I abandoned a novel with such relief, and never have I thought about one so often afterwards.

It was eight hundred pages long. Not until page two hundred did the main character leave his house. Rarely does a writer demand so much patience, and only once before had I given up on a book that everybody else admired.

No sooner had I put it down than a friend told me the second half was gripping. Hardly had she finished speaking when I felt the familiar guilt of the reader who has failed.

So I went back. Little did I know that the slow beginning was the point. Only when you have lived in that house for two hundred pages do you understand what it costs him to leave it. Not only is the second half fast-moving, it is haunting precisely because the first is so still.

Under no circumstances would I call it an easy read. But seldom has a book taught me so plainly that being bored and being wrong are sometimes the same thing.

ex.q: How long was the novel?
Why did the writer return to the book?
o: A friend said the second half was gripping
She had nothing else to read

ex.q: The writer now thinks the slow beginning was a mistake.
What did the book teach her?
o: Being bored and being wrong can be the same

l.intro: Two members of a book club argue about this month's novel.

script.t: Kate, never have I read such a gripping first chapter.
Really? I found it heavy going. Not until page eighty did anything happen.
Only then do you understand the narrator, though.
Rarely have I disliked a narrator so much. He's implausible.
Not only is he believable, he's the most intriguing character I've met this year.
No sooner had I started to like him than he lied again.
That's the point. Seldom does a novel make you doubt everything.
Hardly had I finished it when I gave my copy away.
Under no circumstances would I give mine away.
Then we agree on one thing: it's thought-provoking.

ex.q: What did Erlan think of the first chapter?
What does Kate think of the narrator?
Kate kept her copy of the book.
What do they agree on?

lessons.title: Reading: The book I could not finish

4B.title: The sound of silence
words: The sound of an old floorboard or door
The sound of walking on snow or eating crisps
The sound of water falling slowly in drops
The angry sound a snake makes
Short, repeated knocking sounds, e.g. windows when a lorry passes
A loud, high, unpleasant sound, e.g. car brakes
Close a door loudly and violently
Let out a long breath when tired or disappointed

g.title: Speculation and deduction
g.rule:
Show how certain you are about the present, past or future.

modalsIt must be broken. · She can't have heard. · They might be waiting.
adjectivesHe's bound to complain. · It's unlikely to work.
adverbsShe'll probably come. · He definitely won't agree.

ex.q: It's so quiet. Everyone ___ gone home.
He's ___ to be late. He always is.
They ___ (definitely / not) agree to that.

talk: Which sounds do you love and hate? Why do you think they affect you?
Is silence becoming a luxury? Discuss.

r.text:
In a laboratory in Minnesota there is a room so quiet that visitors rarely manage more than half an hour inside. It absorbs almost all sound, and within minutes people begin to hear what must always have been there: their own heartbeat, the hum of blood in the ears, a faint creak that can only be a joint.

Most people assume that silence would be restful. It can't be, apparently, or at least not in this form. The brain, deprived of information, is likely to start inventing some. Some visitors say they begin to imagine sounds that are not there, such as a tap dripping.

Researchers think this may explain why true silence has probably never existed in human history. Our ancestors would have slept beside a fire that hissed and animals that shifted. A sudden absence of noise must have meant danger.

It might also explain something about modern life. We may not actually want quiet at all. What we are probably seeking is control: the ability to choose which sounds reach us. The neighbour's drill is unbearable. Our own, oddly, is bound to be fine.

ex.q: How long do visitors usually last in the quiet room?
What do people begin to hear?
The brain becomes calmer in total silence.
What are we probably really seeking?

l.intro: A couple try to work out what the noise is.

script.t: Arman, listen. What on earth is that noise?
It must be the pipes. They always hum when the heating comes on.
It can't be the pipes. That was a slam, not a hum.
Then it might be the neighbours moving furniture.
At midnight? They're bound to be asleep. They're both over eighty.
It could have been the window. I may have left it open.
You definitely didn't. I closed it myself. There it is again, a sort of creak.
It's probably the cat. She's likely to be on the wardrobe.
The cat is here, on my feet.
Then it's unlikely to be anything pleasant. I'll get the torch.

ex.q: What does Arman think the noise is at first?
Why can't it be the neighbours, according to Lena?
o: They are bound to be asleep

ex.q: Arman left the window open.
Where is the cat?

Completely full, e.g. a schedule with no free time
Time when you relax and do nothing
Focusing calmly on the present moment
Do something to make waiting pass quickly

g.title: Distancing
g.rule:
Use these structures to report something without claiming it is certain.

seem / appearIt seems that prices are rising. · He appears to have resigned.
passive reportingIt is said that … · She is thought to be …
otherapparently · according to the report · There would seem to be a mistake.

ex.q: The minister ___ to have misled parliament.
___ to the survey, most people feel short of time.
He is believed ___ (leave) the country last week.

talk: Do people really have less free time than their grandparents had? What is the evidence?
How do you waste time, and how do you save it?

r.text:
Ask a colleague how they are and the answer is likely to be "busy". It is said with a sigh, but it appears to function as a boast.

It was not always so. A century ago, leisure is thought to have been the mark of success; the rich were those who had nothing to do. Today the position seems to have reversed. According to one study, people who describe themselves as overworked are perceived as more important.

There would appear to be a cost. Doctors report that patients are increasingly unable to tolerate downtime, and it is claimed that many of us reach for a phone within seconds of being left alone.

It may be that busyness has become a way of avoiding harder questions. A jam-packed diary leaves no room to ask whether any of it matters.

Apparently, the remedy is not a holiday. Those who study the subject suggest something more modest and more difficult: an empty hour, with no purpose at all, in which one is expected to do nothing and is believed to be doing it rather well.

ex.q: What does saying 'busy' appear to function as?
What was the mark of success a century ago?
The text says a holiday is the remedy.
What do researchers suggest?
o: An empty hour with no purpose

l.intro: A presenter interviews a researcher about free time.

script.t: People today say they have no downtime at all. Is that true?
Apparently not. According to our data, leisure time has actually increased.
That seems surprising.
It would appear that we simply feel busier. Days are thought to be more fragmented than they used to be.
Because of phones?
There seems to be a link. It is said that the average person checks one every few minutes.
So busyness is partly an illusion?
It appears to be, at least for some groups. Parents of young children are believed to have lost time, however.
And the fear of missing out?
That is widely claimed to make things worse, though the evidence would seem to be mixed.

ex.q: What does the data show about leisure time?
Why do people feel busier?
Parents of young children are believed to have gained free time.
What does the researcher say about the evidence on FOMO?

lessons.title: Listening: Are we really so busy?

words: Not willing to spend money; mean

Something that costs much more than it should
cost an arm and a leg

Money paid all at one time
Unique selling point: what makes a business special

g.title: Unreal uses of past tenses
g.rule:
A past form does not always mean past time; it can mean not real.

wish / if onlyI wish I earned more. · If only I hadn't spent it.
would rather + subject + pastI'd rather you paid in cash.
It's (high) time + pastIt's time we talked about money.
as if / as thoughHe spends as if he were a millionaire.

ex.q: It's high time you ___ saving.
I'd rather you ___ anyone how much I earn.
If only I ___ (invest) that money years ago.

talk: Can money buy happiness? Argue for or against.
What do you wish you had known about money when you were younger?

r.text:
My grandmother kept her savings in a biscuit tin, and to the end of her life she behaved as though the tin were empty.

She had grown up with nothing. By the time I knew her she was comfortable, but she would cut a bar of soap in two and wished aloud that we wouldn't leave the light on. If only she had spent some of it on herself, we used to say.

I understand her better now. It is as if every family carried a memory of its poorest decade. My father, her son, cannot pass a sale without buying something he does not need, as though scarcity were waiting round the corner. I would rather he didn't; he would rather I minded my own business.

As for me, I earn more than both of them ever did, and I still check the price of bread. It is high time I stopped. I wish I could say that I had.

Suppose we all wrote down what money meant in the house we grew up in. I suspect we would discover that none of us is tight-fisted or extravagant by nature. We are simply obedient.

ex.q: Where did the grandmother keep her savings?
How did she behave?
o: As though she were still poor

ex.q: The writer has stopped checking the price of bread.
What does the writer conclude?
o: Our money habits come from our childhood homes

l.intro: Two old friends talk honestly about money.

script.t: Chris, I wish I'd started saving when I was twenty.
So do I. It's high time we talked about it, to be honest.
I'd rather you didn't tell anyone, but I've been in the red since March.
If only you'd said. I'd have helped.
It's my own fault. I've been living as if money grew on trees.
That flat costs an arm and a leg. Suppose you moved somewhere smaller?
I'd rather not, but it's time I tightened my belt.
I wish I earned more, yet I'm not exactly broke.
If only we'd been taught this at school.
Well, it's time we taught ourselves.

ex.q: What does Madina regret?
o: Not saving when she was twenty

ex.q: Madina wants Chris to tell other people.
What does Chris suggest?
How does Chris describe his own situation?

g.title: Verb + object + infinitive or gerund
g.rule:
The verb decides the pattern after its object.

+ object + toI want you to try. · They persuaded me to stay.
+ object + verb without toShe made me wait. · Let him speak.
+ object + -ingI dislike people telling me what to do.
passive of makeI was made to wait.

ex.q: My coach made me ___ every day.
I'd hate you ___ I was ungrateful.
We were made ___ (fill) in three forms.

talk: Do self-help books and apps work? Describe one piece of advice that helped you.
Who has influenced you most, and what did they encourage you to do?

r.text:
At two in the morning, in a small office above a chemist's, a volunteer answers a telephone. She does not know who is calling, and she will never find out.

The helpline's rules are strict. Volunteers are not allowed to give advice, and the training teaches them to resist the urge. "Everything in you wants to tell the caller what to do," she says. "We are trained to let them talk instead, and to help them hear themselves."

She remembers being told, on her first night, to expect silence. She had imagined people shouting. Instead she heard a man breathing for ten minutes before he managed to say that his wife had died. She let him take his time. She did not ask him to explain.

What keeps her coming back? Not gratitude, since callers rarely phone twice. She says the work has taught her to notice the mundane: a kettle, a clean sheet, a second-hand book. "I used to want my life to be remarkable. The calls persuaded me to want it to be ordinary, and to see that as a privilege."

ex.q: Where is the helpline office?
What are volunteers not allowed to do?
Callers usually phone again to say thank you.
What has the work taught her?

l.intro: A volunteer describes working on a helpline.

script.t: What made you volunteer for the helpline?
A friend persuaded me to try. She wanted me to see what it was like.
Were you trained?
For six weeks. They made us listen to recorded calls and let us practise on each other.
What do callers expect you to do?
Mostly they want someone to listen. We're not allowed to give advice.
Is it hard not to?
Very. I hate people thinking I don't care, but I've learned to let them talk.
What helps people cope?
Often the mundane things. I encourage them to notice a small pleasure every day.
Would you recommend it?
I'd urge anyone to try. It reminded me to be grateful.

ex.q: Why did she volunteer?
o: It was part of her job

ex.q: What are volunteers not allowed to do?
The training lasted six months.
What does she encourage callers to do?
o: Notice a small pleasure every day

lessons.title: Reading: The stranger on the phone

6B.title: Can’t give it up
words: A period without phones and other devices
Move up or down through text on a screen
Move your finger across a touch screen
Watch or listen online without downloading
Add more credit to your phone
The area where your phone gets a signal
A message that pops up on your phone
A moment when you lose emotional control
Thinking about something all the time

g.title: Conditional sentences
g.rule:
Beyond the three basic types.

mixedIf I hadn't started, I wouldn't be addicted now.
alternatives to ifprovided (that) · as long as · unless · supposing · even if
formal inversionHad I known, I would have stopped. · Were it not for my friends, …

ex.q: You can borrow it ___ you bring it back tomorrow.
___ I known how hard it would be, I'd never have started.
If I hadn't missed that flight, I ___ (be) in Rome now.

talk: Is there anything you would find hard to give up? What would happen if you had to?
Are people more addicted to their phones than they admit?

r.text:
Suppose every screen went dark tomorrow. What would actually happen?

In the first hour, very little. Most people would assume the fault was theirs and would restart something. Had the outage occurred thirty years ago, nobody would have noticed at all.

By the afternoon, the queues would begin. If your salary arrives digitally and your card needs a signal, then, unless you keep cash in a drawer, you are effectively penniless. Supermarkets, whose tills are online, would close even if their shelves were full.

Were the silence to last a week, the stranger effects would appear. Provided the electricity held, people would telephone each other, and some would discover they knew no numbers by heart. Neighbours would talk. Had we not handed our memories to a device, we might remember how.

Would we be happier? Probably not for long. As long as we could not reach the people we love, the romance of a digital detox would fade quickly.

Still, if it happened, I would like to think I'd know where my torch was. I don't. It's an app.

ex.q: What would most people do in the first hour?
Why would supermarkets close?
The writer thinks people would be happier for a long time.
Where is the writer's torch?

l.intro: A teenager tells her uncle about a digital detox.

script.t: So you survived three days without your phone?
Barely. Had I known how hard it would be, I'd never have agreed.
What did you miss most?
Scrolling, honestly. If I hadn't deleted the apps first, I would still be checking them.
Supposing your friends had needed you?
They had the landline. Provided you tell people, it's fine.
Would you do it again?
As long as it's not exam week. Even if I wanted to, I couldn't live without notifications then.
Were it not for the school project, would you have tried at all?
No. But if I hadn't tried, I wouldn't be sleeping so well now.

ex.q: How long was Aisha offline?
What did she miss most?
She did the detox purely by choice.
What has improved?

7A.title: As a matter of fact
words: A story or idea that many people believe but is not true
Something you must do because of a rule
Should do, because of a rule (often ignored!)
You did it, but it wasn’t necessary
Strong advice or a warning for now
Form a wrong opinion about someone
Harmful or annoying to other people
Without the tools or skills you need
Ask someone to pay too much
Not connected to what is being discussed

g.title: Permission, obligation and necessity
g.rule:
A wider range than must and can.

permissionWe were allowed to leave. · You may begin.
obligationYou are supposed to check. · We had better go. · I ought to know.
necessityYou needn't come. · I didn't need to pay (so I didn't). · I needn't have paid (but I did).

ex.q: You ___ wear a tie, but most people do.
We ___ so early. The doors were still closed.
You'd ___ check the facts before you post that.

talk: Which laws or rules in your country would you change? Why?
How do you check whether something you read online is a fact?

r.text:
Every workplace has a rule that everybody obeys and nobody can explain. In one hospital, staff were not allowed to use a particular staircase. They were supposed to walk the length of the building instead, and new employees were told that they had better not ask why.

A young doctor asked. It took her three weeks to discover the answer. In 1987 the stairs had been painted, and a notice had forbidden their use until the paint dried. The notice had come down. The rule had not.

Organisations are full of such fossils. We needn't have filled in the second form; the department that required it closed years ago. We didn't need to copy the manager into every message; somebody once did, and it became compulsory by imitation.

Rules ought to be reviewed like stock, argues one consultant. Each should be required to justify itself or be withdrawn.

The doctor is more forgiving. "People must have assumed there was a reason. Mostly there is. You're allowed to check, though. You should."

ex.q: What were hospital staff not allowed to use?
What was the origin of the rule?
The second form was still needed.
What does the consultant suggest?

l.intro: Two colleagues talk about a new company policy.

script.t: Ben, are we allowed to work from home on Fridays now?
We are, but we're supposed to tell the manager by Wednesday.
I didn't need to tell anyone last week. Nobody asked.
You'd better check. The policy became compulsory on Monday.
So I needn't have come in yesterday? What a waste.
You weren't obliged to. You ought to read your emails.
I must have missed it. Are we permitted to claim for the internet?
No. We don't have to use our own laptops, though.
It's a bit inconvenient, but it's fair.
We'd better not complain. It could be withdrawn.

ex.q: When must staff tell the manager?
When did the policy become compulsory?
Saule had to come in yesterday.
What can staff not claim for?

lessons.title: Speaking: As a matter of fact

7B.title: A masterpiece?
words: A stone base that a statue stands on
A work of art made by shaping stone, wood, metal, etc.
Art that fills a space, often with objects or light
Art that doesn’t show real things, only shapes and colours
A painting of objects like fruit or flowers
A picture an artist makes of himself or herself
A copy made to look like the real thing
Remember an important person or event
Too many official rules and forms
A situation where the rules are not clear
Something that takes attention away from the real issue
A small lie to avoid hurting someone
Simple, with clear right and wrong answers

g.title: Verbs of the senses
g.rule:
Sense verbs take different patterns for different meanings.

see / hear + object + verb = the whole actionI saw him paint the wall.
see / hear + object + -ing = part of itI saw him painting the wall.
look, sound, seem + adjective / as ifIt looks unfinished. · It looks as if a child did it.
can with sensesI can see what the artist meant.

ex.q: I heard someone ___ the door and leave.
The portrait looks ___ it were alive.
We watched the artist ___ (work) for a few minutes, then moved on.

talk: Describe a painting, building or photograph you love. What can you see in it?
Who decides what counts as art?

r.text:
A museum in the north recently tried an experiment. Visitors were invited to stand in front of one painting, and only one, for twenty minutes.

Most people look at a work of art for less than half a minute. They see it, recognise it, perhaps photograph it, and move on. The curator wanted to know what happens when we go on looking.

The reports were remarkably similar. For the first five minutes people felt bored and noticed themselves fidgeting. Then things began to appear. One woman saw a figure in the background turn, as it seemed, towards the door. A student heard himself breathing and felt the room grow quieter. Several said the colours looked different by the end, as though the canvas had been cleaned.

Nothing had changed, of course. What they could see had always been there.

The curator does not think this makes the picture a masterpiece. "Almost anything looks extraordinary if you watch it change under your attention. We tried it with a still life of onions. People wept."

ex.q: How long were visitors asked to look at one painting?
How long do most people usually look at a work of art?
The painting changed during the experiment.
What does the curator conclude?
o: Almost anything looks extraordinary with enough attention

l.intro: Two friends visit a modern art gallery.

script.t: Dina, come and look at this. I can't see what it's supposed to be.
It's an installation. I watched a man walk round it three times.
It looks as if someone has left the builders' rubbish behind.
I heard the guide explaining it. It commemorates a lost village.
It sounds rather pretentious to me.
Maybe. But stand here. Can you feel the floor moving?
I can, actually. And I can smell wood smoke.
That's part of it. I saw a child crying a minute ago.
It seems more powerful than the abstract paintings next door.
So you can see why it's genuine art?

ex.q: What are they looking at?
What does the work commemorate?
Oscar can feel the floor moving.
How does Oscar compare it with the abstract paintings?

lessons.title: Reading: Looking for a long time

8A.title: The best medicine?
words: A dark mark on your skin after you hit something
A bubble on your skin, e.g. from new shoes
Extra, unwanted effects of a medicine
An ankle injured by twisting it
Signs that you are ill, e.g. a fever
A doctor who is an expert in one area
Someone who always worries they are ill
Treatments like acupuncture and herbal medicine

g.title: Advanced gerunds and infinitives
g.rule:
Gerunds and infinitives also have perfect and passive forms.

perfect: earlier actionHe denied having taken it. · I seem to have lost it.
passiveI hate being told what to do. · She expects to be promoted.
continuous infinitiveHe appears to be recovering.
fixed expressions + -ingIt's no use complaining. · There's no point waiting.

ex.q: She regrets ___ the doctor's advice last year.
Nobody likes ___ like a child.
There's no point ___ (take) antibiotics for a cold.

talk: Do you trust alternative medicine? Why or why not?
What do you do when you feel ill: rest, work or see a doctor?

r.text:
It is one of the stranger facts of medicine that a tablet containing no drug at all can make a patient better. Having been dismissed for centuries as a trick, the placebo is now being studied seriously.

Patients given a sugar pill often report feeling less pain, and being told that it is expensive seems to increase the effect. More surprisingly, some appear to improve even after having been informed that the pill is inert.

It would be a mistake to conclude that illness is imaginary. A placebo cannot be expected to shrink a tumour or mend a sprained ankle. What it seems to alter is the experience of symptoms, which is worth taking seriously, since being in less pain matters to the person in it.

There is no point pretending this is comfortable for doctors. Prescribing a sham raises obvious ethical questions.

Yet the research points somewhere useful. Being listened to, being examined carefully and being given time all seem to form part of the effect. In other words, some of the medicine may be the appointment.

ex.q: What is a placebo?
o: A tablet with no drug in it

ex.q: What seems to increase the effect?
o: Being told the pill is expensive

ex.q: A placebo can shrink a tumour.
What does the research suggest may be part of the medicine?

l.intro: A patient discusses alternative treatment with her doctor.

script.t: Doctor, I regret not having come sooner. I've been trying herbal remedies.
There's no point feeling guilty. Being worried is natural.
My sister insisted on my seeing a healer. I seem to have wasted three months.
Having tried it, did you notice any side-effects?
Only a rash. I hate being told it's all in my mind.
It isn't. You appear to have a small infection. It's worth treating properly.
I'd like to be referred to a specialist, if possible.
It's no use waiting. I'll arrange for you to be seen this week.
Thank you. I resent having been made to feel like a hypochondriac.
You're anything but. You were right to come.

ex.q: What had the patient been trying?
What did the doctor find?
The doctor thinks she is a hypochondriac.
What will the doctor arrange?

lessons.title: Reading: The pill that does nothing

8B.title: A must-see attraction?
words: So amazing it is almost unbelievable
A famous symbol of a place
Away from where tourists usually go
Pretty, especially in an old-fashioned way
Beautiful because it hasn’t been changed
Full of things designed for tourists
Enjoy the feeling of a place
Rest and get your energy back
Go somewhere to escape daily life
Be planned or expected at a certain time

g.rule:
Formal and informal ways to talk about what is planned.

timetables → present simpleThe tour leaves at nine.
be due to / be to (formal)The museum is due to reopen in May. · The president is to visit.
be about to / on the point ofWe're about to board.
future continuous for arranged eventsWe'll be staying near the old town.

ex.q: The exhibition ___ open next spring.
Hurry up! The guide ___ start the tour.
The minister is ___ meet local leaders tomorrow. (formal)

talk: Plan a three-day trip for a visitor to your region. Say what is arranged for each day.
Do you prefer famous sights or places nobody knows?

r.text:
The viewpoint above the old town opens at six. By seven there is a queue, and by nine the terrace is so full that the view is mostly of other people's phones.

I am due to leave tomorrow, and I had planned to skip it. A friend insisted. "You'll be standing where everyone stands," she said, "but you're to look left, not straight ahead."

So here I am, about to be underwhelmed. Straight ahead is the picture I have seen a thousand times: iconic, breathtaking, and somehow flat, like meeting an actor in a supermarket.

To the left is a laundry line, a boy kicking a ball against a church, and a woman who is on the point of losing an argument with a cat.

The guidebook says the terrace is to be closed next year for restoration, and a ticketed platform is due to replace it. Visitors will be allowed four minutes.

I shall be staying another hour. Nobody else is looking left.

ex.q: What time does the viewpoint open?
What did the friend tell the writer to do?
The writer is impressed by the famous view straight ahead.
What is due to replace the terrace?

l.intro: Two travellers compare notes on a tourist attraction.

script.t: Emma, you're due to visit the old city tomorrow, aren't you?
Yes, the tour leaves at eight. We're to meet the guide by the fountain.
I was about to book the same one. Is it overrated?
I'll be finding out. A friend said the view is jaw-dropping.
I was underwhelmed by the castle. It's on the point of being ruined by souvenir shops.
That's a let-down. I'm planning to go off the beaten track on Friday.
Where to?
A village that's due to open a small museum. It's said to be unspoilt.
I'll be staying two more days. May I join you?
Of course. The bus is to leave at nine.

ex.q: What time does Emma's tour leave?
What did Timur think of the castle?
Emma plans to visit a village on Friday.
What is the village said to be?

lessons.title: Reading: The view everybody has seen

9A.title: Pet hates
words: A young lion, bear or fox

An animal’s feet with claws and soft pads
Animals that might soon disappear for ever
Kept in a zoo or cage, not in the wild
Someone who eats no animal products at all
Mostly vegetarian, but sometimes eats meat
The hard, boring part of a job
like a fish out of water
Someone who keeps surprising things secret
kill two birds with one stone
Achieve two things with one action

g.title: Ellipsis
g.rule:
Leave out words that the listener already knows.

after an auxiliary or modalI said I'd help, and I will.
after toYou can come if you want to.
after and / butShe fed the cat and (she) went out.
so / not for a whole clauseWill it rain? — I hope not. · I think so.

ex.q: I didn't walk the dog, but I should ___.
Is she coming? — I ___.
He asked me to stay, but I didn't want ___.

talk: What are your pet hates: small things other people do that annoy you?
Should people be allowed to take animals into shops and cafés?

r.text:
Almost everyone who owns a dog talks to it, and most would admit they don't expect an answer. So why do it?

One explanation is habit: we address anything with a face. Another is that animals are ideal listeners. They don't interrupt, and they never say that they told you so. You can confess to a cat what you wouldn't to a friend, knowing she won't repeat it, and suspecting she wasn't listening anyway.

Researchers have found that people who talk to their pets are not lonelier than those who don't, though it was long assumed they must be. If anything, they tend to be better at reading other people.

Do the animals understand? Some words, certainly. Dogs can learn dozens. Whether they follow the rest is doubtful, but they respond to tone, and perhaps that is all we want them to.

My neighbour puts it simply. "I tell him my plans every morning. He wags his tail. Nobody else in my life is so consistently in favour."

ex.q: Why are animals ideal listeners?
What have researchers found about people who talk to pets?
o: They are not lonelier than others

ex.q: Dogs cannot learn any words.
What does the neighbour's dog do?

l.intro: Two neighbours discuss a dog.

script.t: Daniyar, I've been meaning to speak to you about the puppy.
I thought you might. Is he barking again?
He is. I asked you to bring him in at night, and you said you would.
I meant to. I keep forgetting, though I know I shouldn't.
My husband wants to complain to the council. I'd rather not.
Please don't. I'll build a kennel if I have to.
You don't need to. Just keep him inside after ten.
I will. He chews everything, but he's getting better.
Is he? I hope so. I do like dogs, honestly.
So do I, more than I expected to.

ex.q: What is the problem?
What does Laura's husband want to do?
Laura asks Daniyar to build a kennel.
What does Laura ask for?
o: Keeping the dog inside after ten

lessons.title: Reading: Why we talk to animals

9B.title: How to cook, how to eat
words: Cut into very small pieces with a grater, e.g. cheese
Cooked gently in hot water, e.g. an egg
Cooked in the steam from boiling water
A bowl with holes for draining pasta
A fine net for separating lumps from liquid
A tool for beating eggs or cream
Hard and making a noise when you eat it
Covered in too much oil or fat
Full of small hard pieces, e.g. a sauce
Soft and light, full of air
Water from the tap, not a bottle
A book with instructions for cooking dishes

g.title: Nouns: compound and possessive forms
g.rule:
Three ways to join two nouns.

noun + noun: the type or purposea recipe book · a wine glass (the object)
's: people, animals, timemy aunt's kitchen · today's menu · a week's holiday
of: things, containers, partsthe end of the meal · a glass of wine (the contents)

ex.q: Could you pass me a ___? I'd like some water.
We had ___ rest before cooking again.
The name ___ the restaurant is hard to pronounce.

talk: Describe a dish you can cook, step by step.
Is cooking a pleasure or a chore for you? Why?

r.text:
My family owns a single recipe, and nobody agrees what it is.

It began in my great-grandmother's kitchen as a lamb stew. Her daughter's version, written on the back of a bus ticket, adds a glass of tomato juice. My mother's copy leaves out the lamb's fat and doubles the onions. Mine uses a pressure cooker, which my mother regards as a moral failing.

Last winter we cooked all four on the same day. It took a kilo of meat per pot and an afternoon's argument. Each cook insisted that hers was the original.

The tasting was done blind, by the children. They preferred the newest one, mine, and then ruined my triumph by explaining that it tasted "like a restaurant".

The great-grandmother's version came last. It was heavy and plain, and after a moment's silence my mother said that it tasted of the winter of 1970.

We have agreed to keep all four. A family's recipe, it turns out, is not a list of ingredients. It is a record of everybody's disobedience.

ex.q: What dish is the family recipe?
What does the writer's version use?
The children preferred the great-grandmother's version.
What is a family recipe, according to the writer?

l.intro: A chef teaches a beginner to make a simple dish.

script.t: Today's recipe is my grandmother's. It's a family dish, not a restaurant one.
What's the first step?
Take a kilo of potatoes and a bunch of spring onions.
Should I use the kitchen scales?
Yes, they're in the cupboard door. Now bring a pan of water to the boil.
And the cheese?
Two hundred grams, grated. It's the chef's secret.
After twenty minutes' cooking, what then?
Drain them in the colander and mash them. Add a spoonful of butter.
It smells wonderful. A minute's work with the whisk?
Exactly. Today's lesson: simple food, done well.

ex.q: Whose recipe is it?
How much cheese is needed?
The potatoes are cooked for twenty minutes.
What is used to drain the potatoes?

lessons.title: Speaking: How to cook, how to eat

words: Making your muscles longer before or after exercise
Lying face down and pushing your body up with your arms
Lying on your back and raising your upper body
A rope you turn over your head and jump over
An exercise class with lots of short, different activities
A very fast end to a race
Someone who describes a sports event live
One shot under par in golf
Start doing something well and confidently

g.title: Relative clauses
g.rule:
Defining clauses identify; non-defining clauses add extra information between commas.

defining: who / which / that, or nothing for an objectthe athlete (who) I admire most
non-defining: commas, never thatHer coach, who is Spanish, retired.
which for a whole ideaHe won again, which surprised nobody.
formal: preposition + whom / whichthe team for which she plays

ex.q: The final, ___ was held in Paris, broke viewing records.
She trains twice a day, ___ explains her results.
The player to ___ the award was given refused it.

talk: Which sport is the most demanding, physically and mentally? Justify your choice.
Are top athletes paid too much?

r.text:
The woman who finished last in the city marathon this year crossed the line nine hours after the start, by which time the barriers had been removed and the road reopened.

She is seventy-one, and she took up running at sixty-five, which most coaches would consider late. The club that she joined, whose youngest member was half her age, did not know what to do with her.

Her trainer, who had worked with professionals, expected her to give up within a month. What happened instead was something for which he had no method: she simply kept arriving. She ran slowly, which irritated the others, and she never missed a session, which irritated them more.

The finish, which nobody filmed, was witnessed by a street cleaner and a taxi driver, both of whom applauded.

Asked what she had learned, she said that the people to whom medals are given are not always the ones who need them. "I wasn't racing them. I was racing the woman who nearly stayed at home."

ex.q: How long did she take to finish?
At what age did she take up running?
Her trainer expected her to succeed from the start.
Who was she really racing?
o: The woman who nearly stayed at home

l.intro: A journalist interviews a running coach.

script.t: You train amateurs, most of whom have never run before. Why?
Because the people who start late often enjoy it most.
Your method, which you developed in Kenya, is unusual.
It is. The runners I coach begin with stretching, which surprises them.
What is the mistake that beginners make most often?
Running too fast, which leads to injury.
The woman whose story you tell in your book started at sixty.
She did. The race in which she finished first was her tenth.
Is there anyone to whom you'd say: don't run?
Very few people. The body, which is cleverer than we think, usually adapts.

ex.q: Who does the coach train?
What do his runners begin with?
Beginners usually run too slowly.
How old was the woman when she started?

lessons.title: Speaking: On your marks, set, go!

10B.title: No direction home
words: Become part of a new community
A quiet place where you can escape
Start living a quiet, stable life in one place
Not value something because you always have it
Someone who isn’t accepted as part of a group
Someone who comes to live in a country

Someone who moves to find work, often temporarily
A long journey by sea or in space
Strongly criticize something as very wrong
Sad because you are away from home

g.title: Adding emphasis (2): cleft sentences
g.rule:
Split a sentence in two to highlight one part.

What … is / was …What I miss most is the food.
It is / was … that / who …It was my sister who moved abroad, not me.
The thing / The reason / The placeThe reason I left was the weather.

ex.q: ___ I love about this city is the people.
It was the language ___ I found hardest.
The reason I moved ___ to be near my family.

talk: If you moved abroad, what would you miss most? What I'd miss most is…
What makes a place feel like home?

r.text:
What gives a migrant away is rarely grammar. It is the small things: the way one counts on one's fingers, the moment at which one laughs.

I have lived abroad for twenty years. What I notice most is not what I have lost but what refuses to leave. It is in dreams that my first language returns, and it is always when I am tired that my accent thickens.

The thing that surprised me was how late homesickness arrives. All I felt in the first decade was relief. It was only after my children were born that I began to miss a country they would never quite belong to.

What they have instead is two of everything: two alphabets, two sets of jokes, two answers to the question of where they are from. The reason they find this easy is that nobody has told them it is hard.

What I have learned is this. It isn't the place you leave that makes you an outsider. It is the habit of comparing. What settles you, in the end, is the day you stop.

When does the writer's accent thicken?
The writer felt homesick in the first ten years.
What settles a person in the end?

l.intro: Two friends who live abroad talk about home.

script.t: Anelya, what is it you miss most about home?
What I miss most is the bread. It's the smell that I can't forget.
For me, it was the language that I missed at first.
The thing that surprised me was how quickly I settled down.
What I find hardest is being seen as a foreigner after ten years.
It's the small things that make you feel like an outsider.
The reason I stayed was the work. All I wanted was a year abroad.
What happened was that a year became a life.
The place where I feel at home now is wherever my family is.
What we take for granted, we only notice when it's gone.

ex.q: What does Anelya miss most?
What did Manneh miss at first?
Manneh planned to stay abroad for many years.
Where does Manneh feel at home now?
